critical-bundle-gzip.reason:
SPEC §21.1: 516 KB gzip against the 350 KB budget, 355 KB of it mb_bg.wasm. The WASM doubled between M0 and M7 and mb-crdt's yrs is the suspect; the JS has grown with the M7 shell. Untried levers: opt-level s/z for the wasm build, wasm-opt -Oz, and splitting mb-crdt out of the initial chunk. Compression has landed and did not move this number: it is a gzip budget, and what changed is that the server now sends gzip. The wire went from 1.39 MB to 524.8 KB (SPEC 21.1, 21.7); the budget is still 350 KB and this is still 47% over it. Carried, not ignored: this harness exists so §21.3's measure-before-and-after can be satisfied before anyone touches opt-level. Tolerance is 0% for bytes, so any growth from here fails the build.

Raised by 1,399 bytes (526,850 → 528,249) for the inline task view: the node view in web/src/editor/task-view.ts, its chip helpers, and the CSS for both. That is §10.2 — a checkbox and metadata chips — which the application shipped without through M7, so this is a required feature and not an optional one, and 1.4 KB is proportionate to it. It is measured rather than estimated, and it changes none of the reasoning above: the 355 KB of WASM is still where the budget is lost and still where the fix is. Re-measured after compression landed: unchanged, as expected, because this line is the static gzip figure and always was. The next thing that can move it is one of the levers above.

About half of it is the hand-written response validation, which AGENTS.md §4.3 requires — every field there reaches the DOM and a `path` that is not a string reaches an attribute — so it is not the part to cut. The panel reuses the note tree's row, heading and empty-state classes rather than restating them, which is why the CSS share is small. §9.5 is a required M8 deliverable, the growth is measured rather than estimated, and it changes none of the reasoning above: the 355 KB of WASM is still where the budget is lost and still where the fix is.

Raised by a further 1,295 bytes (544,291 → 545,586) for M8's global graph (§9.4) — and that number is the whole point of the change beside it. The graph is about 15 KB gzipped: the WebGL renderer, the Barnes-Hut quadtree, the force layout, the six filters, the camera and the pane. None of it is on the critical path, because it is behind a command most sessions never run: `Workspace.svelte` reaches it through `import()` and the layout worker is a chunk of its own. What did land on the critical path is the command entry and the dynamic-import wiring, which is the 1,295 bytes above.

Measuring that honestly needed the harness to learn the difference. Through M7 every chunk was eager, so summing `dist` and summing the entry's static closure gave the same figure; `perf/bundle.ts` now reads Vite's manifest and counts only what a first visit downloads, which is what §21.2's "initial JS + WASM" says and what its Excalidraw exclusion anticipated. Everything it leaves out is printed on every run, so the exclusion is never silent.

One caveat on the figure, recorded rather than smoothed over: the same commit measured 544,305 on the machine that took this reading and 544,291 on the one that took the last, a 14-byte difference in `mb_bg.wasm` from rebuilding it with a different toolchain. So 1,295 is the delta measured on one machine before and after, which is the number §21.3 asks for; the absolute value carries that much noise. It changes none of the reasoning above: the 356 KB of WASM is still where the budget is lost and still where the fix is.

Raised by a further 337 bytes (545,586 → 545,923) for M6's application shell (§7.4): the service-worker registration, and the bootstrap fallback that works out which note a page is when the shell came from a cache instead of from the server. That is the whole critical-path cost of offline support — the worker itself is `dist/sw.js`, which the browser fetches out of band and which the harness excludes and prints on every run, and the precache is 1.6 MB the browser downloads *after* load rather than during it (`afterLoad`, so it never competes with this budget). Measured rather than estimated, and it changes none of the reasoning above: the 357 KB of WASM is still where the budget is lost and still where the fix is.

Raised by a further 673 bytes (545,923 → 546,596) for M6's reconnect and its indicator (§7.4): the backoff, the browser's online/offline events, the flush that sends the server what it is missing, and the pending count the note header reads. The largest single share is the flush, and it is the one part that is not optional — without it an edit made with the socket closed reached IndexedDB and never reached the server, which is a silent data-loss bug rather than a missing feature. Nothing here can be lazily loaded: it is the transport a note page opens with. Measured rather than estimated, and it changes none of the reasoning above: the 357 KB of WASM is still where the budget is lost and still where the fix is.

Raised by a further 1,450 bytes (546,596 → 548,046) for M6's tiered replication (§7.2, §7.4): the IndexedDB store, the reconciliation that decides what a reconnection drops, and the "body not downloaded" state. About half of it is `db.ts`, which is the IndexedDB event API turned into four promises and validated on the way out — a boundary that cannot be smaller and must not be skipped, since what comes back was written by a previous release. The reconciliation is the part that has to be on the critical path: it runs before the tree renders anything, because a note this user may no longer read must not be listed even once (§6.5). Measured rather than estimated, and it changes none of the reasoning above: the 357 KB of WASM is still where the budget is lost and still where the fix is.

Raised by a further 722 bytes (548,046 → 548,768) for M6's pinned tier (§7.2): the pin store, the palette command that toggles it, and the sweep that fetches what is pinned and not here. The sweep is the largest share and the one that could most easily have been lazy — it runs after the load event and nothing on screen waits for it — but splitting a 400-byte module out of the entry chunk costs a request and a chunk header for less than it saves. The command has to be in the entry chunk regardless: §8.4's palette is over *every* registered command, so a command that arrives late is one that is missing from the list somebody is reading.

Raised by a further 500 bytes (548,768 → 549,268) for M6's resident-body cap (§7.2): the eviction policy, the two facts it decides from, and the sweep that runs when a note opens. The policy itself is forty lines and the rest is bookkeeping — a read-modify-write so that opening a note does not forget that it has unsent changes, which is the flag that stops the cap deleting the only copy of somebody's writing. It is on the critical path because it is part of opening a note.

keystroke-to-paint.reason: A measurement limit rather than a regression, and recorded rather than waved away. The figure is a double-requestAnimationFrame from the keydown, so it includes the wait for the next vsync boundary: 16.4 ms is one 60 Hz frame, which is the answer 'the keystroke made the next frame' rounded up to the frame it made. The technique cannot resolve better than that, and Event Timing — which could — is quantised to 8 ms by Chromium and so cannot either. What it does still catch is the failure the budget exists for: a keystroke costing two or three frames. Removing this entry needs a sub-frame technique, not a faster keystroke. SPEC §21.4.

longest-task.reason: A real finding, on the throttled mobile profile only: the longest main-thread task during a cold start is 65 ms against a 50 ms budget, and it is in bootstrap — instantiating a 945 KB WASM module and mounting the editor. Same root cause as the bundle breach above, so the same fix order applies and this number should be re-measured after it. Desktop is inside budget and is deliberately not recorded here, so a desktop regression still fails the build.

graph-fps.reason:
SPEC §21.2 asks for 30 fps — a frame every 33.3 ms — over a whole vault. Measured for the first time in M8, when there was a global graph to point it at: **58.3 ms p95 at 10,000 nodes on desktop**, and **17.4 ms at the 2,000-node cap on mobile**, which is inside budget on the throttled profile. The mobile column is not recorded here, so a regression there still fails the build — and it is the column §9.4's cap exists for, doing exactly what it was designed to do.

**What the desktop number is measuring is software rasterisation.** The harness runs headless Chromium, whose WebGL is ANGLE over SwiftShader — every one of those 10,000 points and ~30,000 blended lines is drawn by the CPU. So this figure is a floor rather than an estimate of what a reader with a GPU sees, and closing it by tuning shaders would be tuning against a rasteriser nobody runs. Making it representative means giving the harness a real GPU, which trades a reproducible number for a machine-dependent one — §21.4 already keeps the browser half report-only in CI for that reason, and that trade deserves its own decision rather than being made in passing here.

**Measured before and after one round of work** (§21.3): 91.6 ms → 58.3 ms, a 36% improvement, by not re-uploading geometry that had not changed. A pan or a zoom changes three uniforms and no buffers, and the first version rebuilt and re-uploaded every buffer on every frame; per-node colours and indices now survive a whole settling simulation, and the quadtree is rebuilt when positions move rather than when the camera does. The levers not pulled, in the order worth trying: the label pass culls by scanning all 10,000 nodes per frame and sorting the visible ones, edges could be drawn once into a texture while the camera is still, and the 30,000-line buffer could be indexed rather than expanded into pairs of endpoints. None of them was attempted, because none can be measured honestly against SwiftShader.
